speechtext: The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved that the House go into Committee of Supply-
['And will the hon. minister please bring the account with respect to West Middlesex.\nProgress reported.']

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I move in amendment that all the words after ' that ' be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
It is greatly in the interest of the market gardeners and the farmers, that the duties on the products of our Canadian gardeners be so readjusted as to assure to the Canadian farmer an adequate protection against foreign competition.
I do not propose to revive the discussion which took place last year in the House on this subject. Some hon. members on the other side stated at the time that I had postponed moving a resolution to the same effect as this amendment, in order to embarrass the government and make political capital out of the question. That was so far from my thoughts that 1 offered to withdraw my resolution if some one on the government side should rise and declare that the government would undertake to have it passed.	.
This year again, I delayed answering the speech made during last session by the hon. member for West York until the last moment, until the latter part of this session. in order to enable him to keep the numerous promises he made on the hustings in the course of the last electoral campaign and to redeem the pledge he took when, at tlie head of a numerous delegation of gardeners from the province of Ontario, he nrged the hon. Minister of Finance to revise tlie tariff in the sense he had pointed out.
If I remember rightly what he said last year to argue himself into voting as he was told and setting aside his promises to His electors and to the gardeners throughout the country, he claimed that having put the resolution on the Qrder paper at the vei .v beginning of the session, I then delayed bringing the matter up for discussion until the government had made known their decision not to change the tariff.
Well. I hope that this year the hon. member for West York will support the amendment. to be consistent with himself and to show his electors that he is willing at least when an opportunity offers, to make good the promises made in election time.
Last year several hon. members took part in the debate on that question. Those who spoke in favour of my motion took the view more especially that the gardeners in the vicinity of Montreal should be more highly protected. I admit that in a question of that kind, both sides should be considered, the interests of the producers as well as those of the consumers. I remember an hon. member saying that for one he was in

476S
favour of the consumer anil would remain so, so long as s me means had not been devised of increasing the production of our gardens in winter time ; so long as the course of the stars had not been changed and a warmer sun given to Canada towards the close of winter.
Mr. Speaker, the number of gardeners in the vicinity of large cities, such as Montreal and Toronto, is larger than is imagined. In the census bulletins, these gardeners do not appear as such ; they are entered as ordinary farmers. In the neighbourhood of Montreal, there are between two and three hundred gardeners, each one of whom employs between five and thirty people. I may say that there are at leas't five or six hundred families who subsist on gardening in the counties of Laval and Jacques Cartier alone. I am told that about Toronto there are at least two or three thousand people who support themselves on gardening.
All these farmers and market gardeners, have to pay heavy duties on everything they consume. They pay duty on the tools they use ; on the clothes they wear. Why should they not in turn be protected like others, as stated in their petition forwarded to the Customs Department ? All they ask for, is that their industry, their business, their labour should be protected as those of other producers. It seems to me they have a right to be heard and to obtain protection from the government.
Last year (April 2S, 1902), the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) made a similar statement On page 3059 of ' Hansard,' I find him quoted as follows
Now, I say, that to my mind is a hardship, and I believe it would be wise for the government carefully to consider this question. I would like to see them increase the duty a'little. I don't think we need go very far, because if the effect of the increase in that duty is to advance the price of these vegetables in the early spring, it is only the well-to-do people who consume them. If you pay a cent, or two cents more for your cabbages to get them in April or May, it is only the wealthy classes that use those goods at that season, it is not the poor people that consume them. Then when our own vegetables come into the market our people will be able to supply the market of Canada with all the goods the consumers require and there is sufficient competition among the market gardeners in Canada themselves to keep the prices right.
These few words suflice to meet the objections raised against my amendment by the bon. members on the other side who are free traders. What do the gardeners ask by their petition, which I have looked into? They request that a specific duty be put on foreign products similar to theirs. At present there is an ad valorem duty ; 25 per cent is paid on the value of vegetables imported from the United States, and in most cases these vegetables are entered as damaged products, and instead of the government getting the full revenue from the duty, Mr. LEONARD.
an insignificant amount only is collected therefrom. Market gardeners request that asparagus be submitted to a duty of three cents per pound ; cucumbers, 20 cents per dozen ; lettuce, 25 cents per dozen ; cauliflowers, 3 cents a piece ; spinach, 25 cents per bushel ; potatoes, 25 cents per bushel ; cabbage, 3 cents a piece, and so forth. I submit to the House this request of the market gardeners, because it appears to me to be fair and reasonable, and because .under the United States tariff, which specially provides for the protection of tlieir farmers against foreign or Canadian competitors, the rates are about as high as those I have mentioned.
As already stated, every feature of this question was discussed in the course of the session. If I remember aright, the hon. Minister of Finance did not say at the time that he was adverse to an increase of duty on these products. He was content with informing the House that the government had not as yet made up tlieir minds as to changing the tariff, and thereupon he moved the adjournment of the debate. Since last session, the hon. Minister of Finance has had plenty of time to study the question, and make inquiry from parties interested and even members who are in favour of an increase in the duties ; and I trust that this year he will comply with the request of the gentlemen I have the honour to represent tonight. My hon. friend, the member for La-belle (Mr. Bourassa) is nodding to me just now, and I infer from his action that he does not agree with me. However, I was pleased to hear him last week in this House state over and over again that he was a protectionist.
I wish to draw the hon. gentleman's attention to tile fact that he is not allowed to refer to a previous debate.

At all events, Mr. Speaker, I know of a good many members who, though unwilling to give themselves out publicly as protectionists, admit as soon as they are outside this House, that they are in favour of protection, and I have heard an hon. member on the other side proclaim himself in this House a protectionist, though he considered he was bound for party reasons to vote in favour of free trade. The market gardeners of Canada are a class of men who are particularly in need of whatever assistance the government can give them in the way of protection. Their calling requires a great deal of industry, a considerable amount of skill, and a market gardener with four or five acres will employ almost as many hands as a farmer with 200 acres. It is such a labour employing industry as this that we ought to protect. Postmaster General in the room of the Minister of Finance, in regard to this question, and on that occasion the hon. member for West York stated that there were upwards of 4,000 people engaged in this industry in the neighbourhood of Toronto. If I have misstated or overstated the figure, I am quite sure the hon. gentleman will correct me. His statement on that occasion deeply impressed me with the importance of the industry in and about the city of Toronto. If that number of people are engaged in it, it is certainly something that should command the attention of the government, and these people should be put in the position of securing that market and thus receive a fair return for their labour and for the money they have invested in lands in and about the city of Toronto, which are very costly indeed ; and the same may be said with regard to Montreal and all the other large cities of Canada. The hon. member for West York appears to have given this question a considerable study. In fact, when lie appeared before the electorate on the occasion of his election in West York, it was largely on the line of increased protection to the market gardeners in and about the city of Toronto. What he says on that question, therefore, I take to be pretty well thought out and perfectly reliable. When he introduced this deputation to the ministers, I understood him to say that the increased cost of the vegetables to the consumers resulting from increased duties would be a mere trifle, amounting to not more than five or ten cents per family per week, which he regarded as a very insignificant matter compared with the great advantage of having this industry fostered and protected in such a way as to give to that large number of people a' profitable return for their labour. The ordinary objection has been raised tonight to an increase in the duty on vegetables-an objection which I regret to say is often raised by the hon. Minister of Finance when proposals are made to increase the tariff-that an increased duty would enhance the price to the consumer. As I have said, the hon. member for West York treated that suggestion as a very insignifi-

cant matter. But if t)je hon. Ministei of Finance would regulate liis tariff in such a way as to foster the industries of this country, I see no reason why any family should be called upon to pay any more if the duty on vegetables were increased. It would be a very easy matter for the Minister of Finance to materially increase the duty on vegetables, even if it did add something to the price, if at the same time he reduced the duties on some things which we cannot produce in the country, such as raisins, currants, figs, and other dried fruits. We do not and cannot produce these dried fruits in Canada, and any taxes imposed upon them are direct taxes for revenue only, and not for the purpose of fostering any industry. The Minister of Finance could take the duty or part of the duty off these articles, and enable the various families throughout the country to get them at less cost, and at the same time he could put an increased duty on vegetables, and give the people who are engaged In that industry a larger market and a better chance of making their livelihood, while the consumers would not have to pay out any more for their living during tlie year.
I notice that the total duty on vegetables - and these do not include potatoes which we do not propose to interfere with at present- was 8815,074 but the total duty which we pay on prunes, raisins and other dried fruits amounted to $304,640, making a slight reduction in the duty on dried fruits would very readily make up for the increased duty on our vegetables.	The same may
be said of small fruit.	The hon. gentlemen who preceded me. having spoken in French, I am not sure whether they included small fruit in tlieir proposition, but I would like to see the duty increased on small fruits, such as raspberries, strawberries and gooseberries, which are grown largely in the county I have the honour to represent. I do not consider that it would hurt the people if we increased the duty, because we might at the same time reduce the duty on sugar. In this way we would encourage an industry which employs a great deal more labour than people imagine, and by reducing the duty on raw sugar produced in Germany, you would not hurt any one. I do not therefore see that It would enhance the cost of living to the families of this country if we should increase the duty on vegetables and give our market gardeners that protection which is so desirable, as the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) has pointed out. We were told a short time ago that the Americans wanted our markets for their small fruits, but as they do not take any small fruits from us, or scarcely any, we gain nothing by the exchange, and it would be quite immaterial, as far as our people are concerned, whether they raise the duties on these articles cr not. With reference to the duty on vegetables going to the United Mr. HENDERSON.
States, as compared with the duties on vegetables coming to Canada, I think we might well come somewhat nearer what the Americans charge us when we endeavour to send them vegetables. I shall only take one article as an illustration of how unfairly our market gardeners are treated. We have to meet keen competition from the other side at a low rate of duty, because I think that 25 per cent on a low priced article is a very low rate. It can scarcely be said to be a revenue producing duty and it certainly cannot be called a ihgli protective duty, whereas the Americans, on the other hand, make their duty practically prohibitive. Take tlie article of cabbage, at three cents per head, the duty on. cabbage going into the United States from Canada is practically 100 per cent, and we admit it at 25 per cent. Why should we not mete out to tlie Americans the same kind of treatment that they do to us ? If they want our market, let them treat us fairly. If they want to come in here in the early season with tlieir vegetables before ours are ready, surely they ought in return to give us similar access to tlieir markets in tlie later season. A 100 per cent against a 25 .per cent is altogether unfair, and tlie Minister of Finance would lie perfectly justified in acceding to tlie request of the hon. member for Unval (Mr. Leonard) by giving adequate protection to the market gardeners around the city of Montreal. Toronto and elsewhere, so as to enable them to make more profit out of tlieir calling, and I may tell you, Mr. Speaker. that there is a larger number of people employed in the production of vegetables and small fruits than any of us Imagine. If the hon. Minister of Finance could see his way clear in granting relief to these people, lie could do so. without imposing any burden on tlie country in tlie shape of increased taxation, because, whilst increasing the duty on the articles we can produce, he c >uld take off a certain amount of duty from articles which we cannot produde and thereby maintain a level < f taxation. I hope therefore that he will not turn a deaf ear to our appeal but will see his way to granting some relief to this hard-working section of our community.

(Translation). Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a word or two In reply to a remark by the hon. member from Jacques Cartier. He first vouchsafed to inform the House that in bringing forward this amendment, tlie lion, member for Laval was redeeming a pledge given to bis constituents during tlie election campaign in liis constituency. Tlie lion, gentleman forgets, no doubt, that another election was taking place at tlie same time in the division of St. James, of Montreal. Those two counties are almost adjacent to each other, and in tlie division of St. James, of Montreal, there was nothing said about garden products, while in

tlie county of Laval, it was the great election cry. The reason is, indeed, that the market gardeners are not the only class concerned. I doubt very much whether the majority of the Laval electors are interested in market gardening. Besides, I think the hon. member for Laval has failed to show that the market gardeners were in as desperate a position as he would have us believe.
I have always been of the opinion that the market gardeners in and around the city of Montreal were among the most prosperous people in the country. I believe that the market gardeners in Montreal are the class of people who have made most money within the last few years. Under the circumstances, with a tariff of 2.1 per cent on their products, is it fair for them to come to parliament and ask for an increase in the customs duties, when tin y are enjoying a prosperity of such, an exceptional character ? It ill becomes them to come come down here and ask for an increase of from 30 to 100, per cent in the duties. They have grown rich under protection, and the least they could decently do, would be to show that their position warrants them in asking for such an increase.
When I go to the market in Montreal and 1 have to pay twenty-five cents for three small tomatoes which I can hold in the hollow of my hand, it strikes me that the price charged is high enough.
Those are American tomatoes.

(Translation). I agree that those tomatoes come from across the line, because there are no Canadian tomatoes for sale in that season of the year. So with cucumbers. We have to buy cucumbers imported from the United States, because our market gardeners cannot grow any in that season.
Although the county of St. John and Iberville be twenty-five miles distant from the zone referred to by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, if it could be impressed upon the farmers of that county that the produce grown by them could fetch such a price, 7 am sure they would engage in that industry.
If our markets were flooded with American products, which were sold at a low price, the hon. gentleman would be justifiable in claiming some measure of protection, on the ground that the Canadian market gardeners were unable to enter into competition with the Americans, owing to the demoralized state of the market. As I said, the prosperity enjoyed by the market gardeners in the vicinity of Montreal is si*c-li that it ill becomes them to complain about the prices of the market. For these reasons, I cannot support the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Laval.

Whatever else the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Leonard) expects in bringing forward his present motion, at least he cannot expect to win the favour of that class of hon. gentlemen who usually differ from him. Of course, it would have been possible for the hon. gentleman to present his motion in a different form, and at one stage of the affairs of this session it seemed that he desired to present it in a different form. I have on another occasion called the attention of the House to what may be called the advantages and disadvantages of proceeding in this particular way in dealing with tariff matters-I mean by a motion in amendment to the usual motion presented by the government for the House to resolve itself into committee of supply. One of the advantages of this form is that it enables the hon. gentlemen who move the motion to have a direct vote on certain matters on which they wish to have a vote, and I cannot blame them for using that form. On the other hand, one of the disadvantages is that it prevents that free and open discussion of the question hon. gentlemen ordinarily desire to have. Now, at an early stage of this session, on the 3rd of April, my hon. friend from Laval placed upon the notice paper a motion in substance the same as this which he presented to-day. That motion, if presented to the House, might have been dealt with ns an open question, for it did not take the form of a non-confidence motion. But my hon. friend, for his own purposes-and I do not at all question his right ; he is the best judge of the method to be used-deliberately allowed that motion to remain on the notice paper for five or six weeks without moving it Ultimately he dropped that motion, and now he comes forward and presents what is in effect the same motion, but he presents it in the form which is the most obnoxious form in which it could be presented to the government and to those hon. gentlemen who are good enough to favour us with their support. I cannot suppose that the hon. gentleman expects the motion to pass, or even to win many votes. He has, by following this method and putting the motion in this form, done his utmost to prevent hon. gentlemen on this side from voting for the motion. The question which the hon. gentleman raised is not new. It was dealt with in a general debate that took place this session, and it was also dealt with last year. Whatever may be said as to the merits of the motion if it arose in connection with a general, or even considerable, revision of the tariff, it has no merits if it is to be selected as one class of imports to be dealt with by the hon. gentleman to-night. If we were dealing with various items of the tariff, making either an extensive or a general revision, the hon. gentleman's views would be entitled to more consideration than we feel we are able to give them now. He lias referred to the fact that my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell) introduced

a large deputation to me early in the session, who urged that some increase be made on the duties on vegetables. I must say, in justice to my hon. friend from West York, that, if we have not made this change, it is through no fault of his, for he has been most zealous in presenting the matter to us, both by the deputation and otherwise. But we have not thought that, at a time when we are not dealing with the tariff, there is any special reason for selecting this particular branch of industry as the subject of special legislation. I think it would not be too much to say that this branch of industry, important as it is, is not likely to be suffering to any large extent. I will not go so far as to say that there is nothing in the contentions of the hon. gentleman, for all these matters are fair subjects for consideration ; but I think that those hon. members who live in large cities and have the pleasure of seeing the market gardeners coming in to the market will agree with me when I say that the market gardeners living near large cities are probably amongst the most prosperous farmers in Canada. They have advantages and opportunities which are not given to many of those in distant rural districts ; and my observation is that the market gardener near a large city is, as a rule, a very comfortable and prosperous person. That is one reason why we do not now select the market gardeners1 as objects of our special consideration or regard.
My hon. friend from Haiton (Mr. Henderson) has referred to the small amount of duty we have collected on vegetables. And very properly so. Why is the duty so collected such a comparatively small amount ? Because the importations are comparatively small. These goods only come in at certain seasons of the year, when our farmers are not producing the goods. If there are seasons when people in more southern climes can produce these things by the hand of nature on more favourable conditions than we, I do not think we should endeavour to shut them out altogether. I venture to think that, even if we increased the duty we should not shut them out altogether; and I doubt if the market gardeners would be substantially benefited, even if the duties were increased. I will say for the hon. member for Haiton that, when he discusses matters of this character, he does not fall into the error into which so many hon. members on his own side of the House do, of thinking that increased duties do not increase the tax and the burden. He accepts the conclusion of his own logic and admits that there will be an increase. But, he says, I will show you how to lessen the burden in some other direction; you may have to pay more for your vegetables, but you can square the account by getting cheaper grapes and figs. These are commonly regarded as luxuries; and I am inclined to think that the working man will hardly agree to make his vegetables more Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
expensive that he may get his compensation in buying his grapes and figs at cheaper rates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: The hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has never been in the grocery business, or he would know differently.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Henderson) has been in the grocery business, I infer from what he says. But, in spite of his superior knowledge, I venture to say that for one man who buys figs and grapes, there are ten men who buy the common articles of vegetables. Therefore, any attempt to increase the price of vegetables and square the account by making the price of figs and grapes cheaper will, I think, hardly be the popular policy that he believes it to be. There is another point in which the hon. gentleman is ready to make a reduction-and I would like to hear the hon. gentleman on these matters, for he is always ready with proposals. He is not lacking in fairness. He says :	I want to do this, and if there is a
disadvantage in it, I will show you how to make it up. Well, he is going to cheapen figs and grapes-
Currants and raisins.

Yes. in justice to the workingman, I must put in currants and raisins; I certainly would not keep them out of his cake even if I could. The hon. gentleman says : Tl ere is another duty you can reduce. In proposing it. he wants to get even with the people of the United States and put a check on something that they send us. But what he proposes is to reduce the duty on German sugar. At the very moment when this country is ringing with admiration for the policy of this government in increasing the tax on German goods, the hon. gentleman coolly comes in and makes the proposal that we shall reduce the duty on German sugar. Apart altogether from the lack of logic in the hon. gentleman's position, apart from his failure to appreciate the national sentiment in the policy of this government, apart from his failure to appreciate the policy which has not only won the admiration of the people of Canada, but has won the admiration of the people of the whole empire, for we have asserted our right to be a portion of the empire free from any action that Germany may take ; apart from all this, there is another question which the hon. gentleman has forgotten. At the moment when he is pressing us to reduce the duty on German sugar, deputations from his own province of Ontario, consisting of those interested in the beet-root industry, are asking us to increase the duty on German sugar.

Give them a bounty.

I am bound to tell the hon. gentleman that they have asked not only a bounty but an increase of duty also, and, of the two they would prefer the increased duty. So, my hon. friend in his proposal-and I give him credit for readiness in replying-met the difficulty arising out of giving the workingman dear vegetables by saying that he would give him cheap figs
No.

Yes, and at the moment when we are bound, in the interests of the country to resent the action of Germany, he comes forward and proposes that we go back on that policy and reduce the duty on German goods. At the very time when the beet growers of his own province are coming and asking us for increased duty on sugar, my hon. friend, who thought he was a high protectionist, comes and asks us to reduce the duty on German sugar. However, I do not wish to go into a general discussion of the tarif. Be it wise or be it unwise, the government have said that they do not regard it as expedient for the present session that we should enter into any extensive tariff changes; and unless we were entering upon general or extensive tariff changes there is no good reason for selecting this particular item as the subject of special consideration. If it were necessary to make comparison, there are other interests in Canada, probably not so well off as our friends the market gardeners, who, I think, as a rule, are by no means the least prosperous of Canadian citizens. However, since the hon. gentleman from Laval has withdrawn his original motion which would have allowed a general discussion of the question and has brought it forward as a vote of want of confidence, he will hardly expect any hon. gentleman on this side to vote for it. At all events, with every desire to appreciate the position of the market gardeners of Canada, I am bound to tell the hon. gentleman that I am unable to vote for his motion.

It is becoming difficult for my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) to keep his followers in line. The only way he has been able to do it for some weeks past is by appealing to them to vote down motions of want of confidence. Yet, only three years ago, there was a motion introduced by my hon. friend from Hants (Mr. Russell) with regard to the British preference which was not regarded as a vote of want of confidence, though it possessed every element in that respect of the motion of my hon. friend the member for Laval (Mr. Leonard). It is very difficult indeed to please the bou. Minister of Finance. Introduce a general motion with regard to the tariff, and he tells you it is too general; he may even tell you that he does not know what it means; he
cannot understand it. Speak, for instance, of adequate protection, and the hon. gentleman cannot understand it; it is a meaningless phrase to him. But he has no trouble whatever in understanding legitimate protection when that expression is used by the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine). And a few years ago, he assailed a former Conservative government because it had not given to the c-oal mines of Nova Scotia anything that could be regarded as adequate protection.
Well, he is not satisfied with a general motion, and you would think you might satisfy him with a specific motion, but when you come with a specific motion it satisfies him too well, it is too specific, and because it is not general, because it does not deal with every article in the tariff, he calls upon his followers to vote it down. In what way is this motion of my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard) inopportune ?-I think that is the proper expression, every one of these specific motions is inopportune. If it is a motion of a general character it is vague and indefinite ; if it is a motion of a specific character it is inopportune. Why. Mr. Speaker, I suppose that every hon. gentleman in this House, every one who looks over the history of this country during the past twenty-five or thirty years, knows that motions with regard to the tariff have been introduced almost invariably as amendments to motions to go into Committee of Supply. If I am not mistaken, the policy of the Conservative party in the time of Sir John A. Macdonald between 1874 and 1S78. was presented to the country by a motion in exactly the same way in which the hon. member for Laval has presented this motion to-night.
But there is another very curious thing in connection with this. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance says :	Why did you
not put this motion on the Order Paper in the ordinary dourse ? He says that my horn friend from Laval had such a motion on the Order Paper. Well, it is true he had that motion on the Order Paper, and he also had one of a similar kind last year. But what became of that motion ? Why, the Minister of Finance shelved it himself by a motion to adjourn the debate, knowing it would never come up again, in order that certain followers of his who did not care particularly to vote against that motion, might not be put in an awkward position by having a vote taken upon it in the House. To-night he calls upon them to vote this motion down because it is a motion of want of confidence, and because, I suppose, it is inopportune. Well, the Minister of Finance does not put himself in a very good light, it seems to me. If my hon. friend from Laval had proceeded with his motion this year, the Minister of Finance, after a certain amount of debate had gone on, would have risen again and moved the adjourn-

ment of the debate, and the motion of my hon. friend might have been shelved. That would have been his procedure, and I challenge him to say that he would not have done exactly what he did last year.
Very likely I would.
And yet he complains.
I do not complain.

Then, Mr. Speaker, I do not know what you would call complaining. It is something very much like it. He seemed to tind fault-let us put it in that way-he seernd to lind fault with my hon. friend from Laval because he has put this motion before the House in the only way in which be could do it for the purpose of obtaining and having recorded the votes of hon. gentlemen in this House on the merits of that motion. Now the motion is specific, it is true. Hon. gentlemen on the ether side have been shouting for specific motions, have been declaiming against the so-called vague motions that have been made in the House with regard to the tariff, they have been clamouring and thirsting for these various specific motions which are being presented to them during this session. When they get these specific motions for which they have been thirsting so much during the past two or three years, they do not seem to be any better satisfied with them than they were with the motions couched in more general terms which have been presented to the House during the past two or three sessions.
The Minister of Finance seems to think that no labouring man in this country lias a right to be in a position to use figs or grapes ; he seems to think these articles of food should be reserved for gentlemen in the position of cabinet ministers, or in a similar high scale of life. Well, I can tell the hon. gentleman that I think the labouring man of this country fcr the most part have a right to aspire occasionally to buy a basket of grapes containing ten pounds for twenty-five cents, and I think as I am reminded by my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) that those grapes which are grown in Canada and sold at a very small price, are a very good article indeed.
I do not know that there is any reason why these articles should not bo protected in accordance with the terms of the motion presented by my hon. friend from Laval. The Minister of Finance,-although he thinks the labouring man has no right to aspire to grapes or figs, seems to think that he may aspire to the luxury of early vegetables, or strawberries in February, and tomatoes in February or March. Well, I should lie very glad indeed to see the labouring men of this country in a position to have these articles, but for the most part these articles, at that season of the year, are in every sense Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
of the term luxuries, and are only used by people in this country who are in a position to command luxuries. A tax such as that proposed by the hon. member for Laval to-night would not bear upon the working people of this country, because these articles at that season of the year when they cannot be produced in Canada, are not used to any extent by labouring people.
There was not anything else in the remarks of the Minister of Finance, as I recollect them at this moment, which are deserving of any answer. I can only say that my hon. friend from Laval is perfectly justified in placing this motion before the House in the way which he has done to-night, by reason of the tactics employed by the Minister of Finance in this House last year to avoid the taking of a vote upon this very question, and if he had taken the course suggested by the Minister of Finance, that gentleman, according to his own very candid avowal to-night, would have adopted the same tactics to prevent a vote being taken upon this motion to-night. Therefore there can be no possible excuse for the government complaining of the conduct of my hon. friend, or saying that this motion calling for a certain reform in the tariff should necessarily be regarded as a motion of want of confidence.

Before the vote is taken I would like to say a word on this subject. The leader of the opposition complains of the course taken by the Minister of Finance, in reference to the motion which was presented last year, in moving the adjournment of the debate and thus shutting off a vote on the original motion. Now it will be remembered that last year the hon. member for Laval put his notice on the motion paper, I think on the second day of the session. It was called week after week and month after month, and either he was not here, or it was allowed to stand for two months and a half before he brought it up. In the meantime the budget speech had been delivered and the government had come to the conclusion, and parliament had agreed with them, that there should be no changes in the tariff last session. Then during the last days of that session, when no possible good could come from the motion at all, the hon. member for Laval brings it forward, not with the hope of benefiting the market gardeners at all, but with the hope of making a little cheap popularity for himself at the expense of some of those politically opposed to him. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) and some other members during the recess had a good deal to say about the course pursued by me last year in voting for the adjournment of the debate. I approved of that course, and I am prepared now to justify my course, and will be prepared to justify it at any time the hon. member for Peel or

any other hon. gentleman on that side chooses to come and debate the question with me, I justified the course I took then, and I am satisfied that the electors of West York sustained me in the course I took. Not only that, but there is not an hon. gentleman in this House who has advocated the cause of the market gardener more earnestly and more sincerely than I have done. I did it at the right time and in the right place. * It is true that so far I have not been successful, but the time is short. This is only the second session that I have had the honour of representing any of the market gardeners of this country and this session is not over yet. There will be plenty of time, and I still hope that some justice will be done to the market gardeners. What do we see now ? Here, we find, as the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) says, the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Leonard) comes forward again with precisely the same motion-that he put upon the Order paper on the 3rd of April. This motion was called over and over again. Where was the hon. member for Laval ? Absent from his place in this House before the budget speech was delivered at a time when he could have impressed upon the government the justice of liis cause, when he could have given sufficient reasons and perhaps could have influenced the government to grant the redress which he now so earnestly advocates. He allows three months to pass by from the time that he put his motion on the Order paper on the 3rd of April. He drops his motion and now he brings it forward at a time when no amendment can be moved and when no adequate expression of the House can be had upon it. If he had brought it forward in the ordinary way. if he had proceeded with his motion it would have been open for every hon. member in the House to vote as he sawT fit. But, now. what does it mean ? No matter how friendly a member may be to the market gardeners, no matter how anxious he is to see their condition improved it involves voting for this motion of want of confidence in the government, and putting the government out and putting whom in their places? -that outfit over yonder. From the market gardeners standpoint how would their position be improved ? To whom do the market gardeners owe their present condition ?. To thei Liberal party ? No, the Liberal party came into power in 1896. They revised the tariff but they left the tariff exactly as it was before.
Hear, hear.

So far as vegetables are concerned they left the tariff exactly as it was before. They made no change at all. The tariff was higher on vegetables. Who reduced it ? The Conservative party in 1894. When they revised the tariff, and it was the very last revision they made, they
reduced the duty on vegetables. Di,d the hon. member for Haltou raise his voice in protest against it then ? Did the horn member for Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) V
No, did you ?
They were in power, and they supported the reduction of the tariff in 1894.
Did you not ?

The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) was not here then, but, I suppose, if he had been here he would have supported his party too. The hon. member for Laval was not here then. But, I say that if the market gardeners are suffering in any particular they owe it to the Conservative party and not to the Liberal party. 1 believe that a readjustment of the duty should be made. I think it would be in the interest of the people of this country if the duty on vegetables was raised somewhat.
Why not vote for it ?

I believe that the benefit that the market gardeners are to this country is very great indeed. I have no fault to find with the argument that has been advanced by the hon. member for Hal-ton with which I largely agree. There is no doubt that the market gardeners are helping to build up this country. We are endeavouring to get immigrants to come to this country, we are offering inducements to people to come and take up land and settle and build up the country. It is a fact that a market gardener with four or five acres will employ perhaps more help than a man will on 100 or 200 acres of land. They are a very industrious, economical and hard working people. Their remuneration is not very great to-day, and I believe that we can increase their prosperity without, as I said before, increasing the price. It may be that certain times in the year, particularly in the early spring when vegetables are scarce, that the price would be a little advanced if the duty were raised, but, as I pointed out before, at that season' of the year it is very largely the wealthy classes who use vegetables and a little advance in the price would not signify very much. But, the trouble is that when our own market gardeners are able to supply the market they find it flooded with foreign products, and therefore they are deprived of a market they should enjoy. They do not complain so much about the price as that they have not the market. I think if we could increase their market by shutting out the large quantity of vegetables that come in from the United States, it would be better for them. Another point is that the inspection and appraisement of vegetables are not as they should be. Indeed, it is a very difficult thing to arrive at just what the proper value of some of these vegetables

is, and I would ask the lion. Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson) particularly to see that in the appraisement of vegetables coming into the city of Toronto the importers are compelled to pay the proper duty upon the real value of the article introduced. I had the honour in the early part of the session of introducing a large deputation to the lion. Minister of Finance and some other members of the government, and I thought that we made out a very strong case. We presented the arguments in favour of an increase in the tariff ns strongly as we possibly could. We pointed out many things wherein there seemed to be an anomaly. For instance, we pointed out to the government that the American duty on beans was forty-five cents a bushel, while our duty was only fifteen cents a bushel. We pointed out that on prepared pease the Americans have a duty of two and a half cents a pound, on cabbages, three cents per head; hops, twelve cents per pound, onions, forty cents per bushel; pease, forty cents per bushel dried; pease, thirty cents per bushel, split pease, forty cents per bushel; potatoes, twenty-five cents per bushel and on many other things we find that the duty imposed by the United States is very much larger than the duty imposed upon these articles when imported into Canada. Our market gardeners, especially those in West York, hold that if the United States duties were as low as the Canadian duties they could send a good deal of their fruits into the cities of the State of New York, and they complain, and with reason, that they are unable to send any of their products to the United States, while the American gardeners are able to take advantage of the Canadian market. I have strongly pressed, not only upon the Minister of Finance but on other ministers, the advisability of increasing the duty. I believe that if the government, as was stated by the Minister of Finance to-night, had gone into a general revision of the tariff our representations would have had effect, but whether wisely or unwisely they decided they would not make any changes in the tariff this year and we had to abide by the decision they arrived at. I am still in hopes that the tariff will be increased on these articles. I am not going to give up yet; I am going to continue, and I warn the Finance Minister now that I shall be after him again and again. I believe the duty should be increased to help the market gardeners. It would be a grand thing for the country, it will be a grand thing for all those engaged in that trade when the duty is inereased.-So far as I am concerned, I am not going to vote for this motion.

Hear. hear.
Other hon. MEMBERS. Oh.
I am not going to vote against this government.

Hear, hear.
Other hon. MEMBERS. Oh.
I am not going to vote against this government and put the Conservatives into power.
Hear, hear.
I have no confidence in these gentlemen opposite; I do not think they possess the instinct of government.
Oh.
They made a very bad mess of it when they were in power. They were in power too long and the people of Canada spewed them out of their mouths.
Oh.

They will be in opposition a good many years yet before they get the reins of government. When I look around and see the enormous progress that has been made in this country for the last six years-our manufacturing establishments going forward by leaps and bounds, our Great North-west filling up with hundreds of thousands of settlers; the Order Paper of the Railway Committee loaded down with applications for charters to build railways; no country in the world, no British possession making such progress; when I see all this occurring under the wise administration of this government and under the business ability and statesmanship they have shown, I would be foolish indeed to vote to put this government out and to put in power a set of men who have Shown that they were incompetent to manage the affairs of Canada.

Hear.
Other hon. MEMBERS. Oh.

And so, Sir, while I believe in increased protection for the market gardeners and will support their claims in season and out of season, I do not believe I would benefit them by voting against the government. I hope, Sir, that I will be able before long to impress upon the government the necessity for taking some action in that regard. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Leonard) put a motion on the Order Paper on the 3rd of April, and he has allowed it to lapse for two and a half months through his being absent, although it was called over and over again; if he had gone forward with that motion I would have supported it, but he has placed me in a position to-night, so that I cannot support him, much as I believe the market gardeners should get protection.

The hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Campbell! has taunted my hon. friend (Mr. Leonard) with trying to make political capital out of this, but if there is any man in this House who has benefited by political capital more than another, it is my hon. friend from

West York (Sir. Campbell). It is known all over Canada tliat in the by-election in West York he made a direct promise to the market gardeners that if he came to this House they would get protection, and the reason he gave for that was that he was a friend of the government. I question if he would ever have been returned but for that promise. But the government have turned him down, and turned him down frequently, and still he eulogizes them. Well, that is the kind of man the government will turn down and that is the kind of man whose representations will have very little weight with the government. He is a much smaller man to-night than when he came to this House several years ago. What apology does he make to-night for going back on his promise ? He says that if this motion were in proper form he would vote for it. Well, there is nothing to hinder him from implementing his promise-sincere promise supposed to have been-to the market gardeners of West York, and moving a resolution in any form he pleases.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) tells us that if this motion had been moved on the 3rd day of April he would have voted for it-if it were moved on the first of April it would have suited him better.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman says that the miserable set of Conservatives that were spewed out of the mouths of the people in 1896, left the tariff so that the Liberal government could not improve it. Well, Sir, the Minister of Finance has stated to-night that the market gardeners are among the most prosperous people in the country, and if they are prosxierous they are prosperous under the tariff that was adopted by the Conservative government, to whom the member for West York has referred in such undignified language. Any sensible man knows-I do not know whether the member for West York does or not-that the tariff on these garden products should be high, for the reason that the market gardener does not know but that the market which he meets in the morning will be demoralized before ten o'clock in the day by a large importation of American products. The market gardeners of Canada are willing to accept the same tariff that protects the American gardeners, and if the government acceded to that demand, then the radius of market gardening around the cities would extend from twenty miles to thirty miles and even greater, because of the facilities which the railways afford for shipping this produce to market. But what do we find ? We find that when there is a surplus of these articles on the market, they virtually become worthless, because they are perishable articles and must be sold ; and that is why this class of
people should get greater protection than others. The people engaged in this business are willing to invest their capital for the purpose of putting on the market earlier in the spring such articles as lettuce, celery and radishes, if you will secure to them the market against the American product. There is nothing to hinder them raising these articles under glass and putting them on the market at a comparatively low price, except the fact that you allow the American producer to come in with his southern stuff, to a certain extent, decomposed-and I question whether it is yrise to let much of that class of articles come in at that period of the year. The hon. member for West York says : These people ought to have more protection, but I cannot vote for it ; I cannot do my duty to my constituents-oh, no ; I would rather support hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches than do my duty to my electors. So long as we have a sentiment of that kind guiding members of this HousS, this eouutry will suffer : and I am afraid, from what we see here, and from what has been thrown out by the Finance Minister, that is the kind of stuff most of them are made of. Well, we will have to put up with it-their principles are nowhere.
For a long time.

Do not be so sure. There are a good many of you uneasy to-night. You are more afraid of lettuce, carrots, 'mangolds and cabbages!, than you may think you are. Every mother's son of you is a little afraid that the radish will l>e too hot. With all the prosperity we talk about, our hon. friend could not show that tlie cabbages of West York grow a bit bigger than they did before he represented them. The hon. member for West York says he would vote for this motion if it came at the proper time. If the hon. gentleman put himself right with his constituents, I suppose lie would not be sure whether the market gardeners of West York would be left out of the redistribution or not ; and he throws out this sprat to these people, and says : We will perhaps do right by you at another time. The hon. gentleman should be prepared to stand up and carry out his promise to his constituents. He has been here ever since the by-election in the last parliament, and he has never yet moved a resolution to carry out that promise, and it is quite time that he put something on the Order Paper along that line, or cease eulogizing the men he supports.

I would like to ask the hon. member for Dundas if he would be willing to allow the same kind of protection to the market gardeners of British Columbia, to those around my own city, for instance, as he would to the market gardeners around Ottawa and Montreal ?

My hon. friend is altogether too provincial. I am speaking for

Canada, not for British Columbia or Montreal.
The hon. gentleman specified Toronto and Montreal. The hon. gentleman has not answered the question entirely to my satisfaction. I think he should answer it.
I can easily put the hon. gentleman's conscience at rest, if it is troubling him. We are advocating a law that will affect all Canada. That ought to cover British Columbia.

I accept the hon. gentleman's answer. As he is quite in favour of protecting the market gardeners of British Columbia, I may say that our market gardeners are Chinamen. We have practically no white men in our country engaged in that business. I only wanted to know the hon. gentleman's policy on the Chinese question.

I think I ought to say in reply to our hon. friend that it is a pity that the people he speaks of have not a representative here.

There is not the slightest doubt about the understanding. The arrangement was that anything which would be open for discussion on the item we consented to pass, should be open for discussion on the census or any other convenient item.
Has the hon. minister had any correspondence with any person in New Brunswick with respect to the census as it relates to the different religious denominations in that province.

Yes, I have had one or two letters on that subject. The other day I received a letter from the Rev. Mr. McLeod of Fredericton, in which he says that he had proved certain mistakes in the census with regard to the Baptist denomination in New Brunswick, and asked whether any steps would be taken to investigate. I have not yet been able to answer that letter.
Was there not considerable correspondence between the Rev. Mr. McLeod and Mr. Blue, with respect to that particular denomination ?

Y'es, Mr. McLeod had quite an extensive correspondence with Mr. Blue, and Mr. Blue showed successfully that the census was exactly in accord with the information given the enumerators by the people. He also pointed out that in certain comparisons which were made between the returns of the Baptist community in the census of 1891 and 1901, the grouping of that denomination in the census of 1891 comprised other branches than were comprised in the grouping in the census of 1901. Consequently the apparent decrease in numbers of the branch which Doctor McLeod referred to was not due to any difference in the figures of the two censuses.

The denomination of Free Baptists is a very considerable denomination in New Brunswick and the other mari-'lol
time provinces as well. In the county I have the honour to represent it is a very considerable body, yet according to the census its numbers are very inconsiderable. There was a considerable amount of correspondence between Doctor McLeod and Mr. Blue in connection with the parish of Kars, where a very small number of persons were given as belonging to this denomination, whereas, as a matter of fact, the larger portion of that parish belongs to it. The enumerator for that parish admits that he did not put those people down as he should. Doetor McLeod asked that the census be remedied in that respect but could get no satisfaction from Mr. Blue. In the city of St. John, this same religious denomination has a large number of adherents, and so dissatisfied were the ministers of that denomination in that city with the census returns that they numbered their congregations themselves and I have here a statement which shows what little reliance we can place on the census.
Commissioner Blue could find only 410 Free Baptists in St. John city. The. Sunday school census takers found 1,826. In the north end where the census reported 130, ltev. D. Long, pastor of the Victoria street church, has discovered over 700. On the west side, where the census returns report 95 Free Baptists, Rev. Mr. Ferguson has a list of 597. In St. John, south, Rev. C. T. Phillips finds 529, whereas Mr. Blue refuses to allow more than 176. The two-priced census would seem to he a rather poor affair, even at half price.
If this census of Mr. Blue's is not more correct with respect to other matters, it is rather a blue affair. It does seem to me that this is a matter of some importance. It is of importance to a very considerable number of people throughout the province of New Brunswick at least. I do not know whether the same defects occur in other provinces, but, it seems to me that these people hare rights that this government is bound to respect. And if this denomination has lost so much ground by the census of 1901 as compared with the census of 1891, I think it is incumbent upon the minister to show how this has occurred, and also to have another census, even at the very expensive rate of the one he has taken.

I may say, in general terms, without going into the details, that the Rev. Mr. McLeod wrote to Mr. Blue and was replied to. He drew attention to certain apparent discrepancies in the returns of the two censuses. It was pointed out, however, to the Rev. Mr. McLeod that, in the census of 1891 the term ' Free Will Baptist ' was used. The section or branch of the denomination to which Mr. McLeod referred, and to which, I believe, he belongs, used to be called the ' Free Christian Baptist,' but they are row called ' Free Baptist.' In the census of 1891 'Free Will Baptist' and 'Free Baptist ' were used as well as the term



' Baptist.' Certain portions of the Baptist denomination were placed under the heading ' Free Will Baptist,' but others were placed under the heading ' Baptist,' without any further designation. In the census of 1901, the same course was pursued. But in the census of J.891, as I understand it, there were five different branches of the Baptist denomination placed under the head of ' Free Will Baptist ' ; but in the census of 1891 only three branches were placed under the head ' Free Will Baptist ' or ' Free Baptist ' ; and the discrepancy which appears so great in the number of Free Baptists in the province of New Brunswick .is entirely due to that fact. In the explanation sent to the Rev. Sir. McLeod, Mr. Blue drew attention to this fact, and gave figures which showed clearly, that not only had there been no decrease in the numbers of the branch of the denomination to which Mr. McLeod belonged, but, as a matter of fact, there had been an increase of fifty per cent, and that the complaints made of discrepancies which showed a discrimination against that particular branch were not justified by the facts. I merely reply in these general terms, but I have all the details of the correspondence under my hand and could give them to the House if lion, gentlemen desire it. But, of course, it would take a little time.

I think the hon. minister is wrong in his statement. In the first place, though I do not profess to be well posted theologically, I think I am safe in saying that there are not five branches of the Free Baptist Church. I do not know that there are any branches of that particular church; it is a church by itself known as the Free Baptist Church. There is also the Baptist Church. If the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) were here, lie could give more definite information with respect to the denomination. But the Free Baptist Church is as distinct from the Baptist, as is the Methodist, the Congregational, the Presbyterian, or any other branch of the Christian Church. So, the explanation that the hon. minister gives is not an explanation that at all fits the case. As I understand it, in this correspondence that took place between the Rev. Dr. McLeod, who is chief editor of the newspaper organ of this church, and Mr. Blue, Dr. McLeod's complaints were treated rather curtly, and I do not think that Mr. Blue used him with the courtesy which liis position and the cause he was championing called for. I think the correspondence between Dr. McLeod and Mr. Blue should be laid upon the Table, so that we may have the advantage of wliat was set forth on either side.

I assure the hon. gentleman I shall be very glad Indeed to lay the correspondence on the Table, and even to have it printed, if Hon. Mr. FISHER.
necessary. Unfortunately this controversy arose, and the statements concerning it which appeared in the paper of whicli Rev. Mr. McLeod is the editor, were accompanied with only meagre extracts from that correspondence, the effect of which was to misrepresent the actual facts. I do not say that this was the design, but that was the result, as shown by perusal of the articles whicli appeared in the newspapers, which certainly gives a false impression of the correspondence and of the facts of the case. But, for the information of the hon. gentleman, I think it is perhaps just as well that I should read the statement which was sent to Rev. Mr. McLeod, which will show, I think, pretty clearly the facts of the case.
If the hon. gentleman is to read that, perhaps he had better read also Mr. McLeod's side of the correspondence, so that we may have both sides together.
I can read Mr. McLeod's letter, to which this is an answer, and, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) wishes, I can have copies of the whole correspondence laid on the Table.
That would be better.

To place the matter before the House, I think it well that I should read this statement. Mr. McLeod wrote the following letter, and in it raised this whole question. There were several letters between it and the one I have just offered to read, but the one I have just offered to read is in reality a summing up of the case. He drew the attention of the Census Bureau to the matter in these terms :
Census Bulletin No. 5, dealing with the religions of the people is before me.
In the classifications of nominations I find ' Baptists (free will),' 24,229-a falling off of 20,887 since 1891.
Permit me io call your attention to two or three things :
1.	There is no body of Christians in Canada whose name is Free Will Baptisis.
2.	There is a denomination whose corporate name is Free Baptists, and of this body there is a conference in New Brunswick and one in Nova Scotia.
3.	I speak especially for the Free Baptist Conference of New Brunswick, of which I am the corresponding secretary.
4.	The figures you announce for New Brunswick Free Baptists are certainly wrong. The reports from churches in 1890- the last year of the decade with which the census deals-gives us a church membersnip of 12,352 in this province. Yet the census gives us only 15 .'02 adherents in the provioee-3,150 more than we have church members reported. A fair estimate (two and a half times as many adherents as church members) would give us over 30,000, instead of the 15,502 with which the census credits us.
5.	Is there a way by which we can get a more correct showing in the census returns ?
