6. Will you kindly furnish me with a copy of the form on which the facts about the religions of the people were taken by the enumerators t
There was an answer to that on June 3rd from Mr. Blue, and in that he sends back the instructions Mr. McLeod asked for, Mr. McLeod wrote again on June 5th, and Mr. Blue replied on June 15th. Mr. McLeod wrote again on January 16th, 1903, and Mr. Blue replied on February 5th. Then Mr. McLeod wrote again on February 7th, and Mr. Blue on March 21. Mr. Blue writes to Mr. McLeod on March 21, 1903 :
I have spent some time in an investigation of the records with the object of ascertaining as accurately as possible the cause of the apparent discrepancy in the number of Free Will Baptists aud Free Baptists in the Censuses of 1891 and 1901.
Our schedules and compilation sheets ot the 1901 census have been very carefully revised and the result is the discovery of two mistakes made by one of our clerks in preparing the final table from the compilation sheets. In oEe case 472 persons recorded as Free Calvinistic Baptists in the town of Marysville, were added to Calvinistic Baptists and grouped in the table with Baptists. In another case, in King's county, twenty-nine persons recorded as Calvinistic Baptists (presumably Cresrite) and one Old Baptist were added to Free Baptists instead of to Baptists. These corrections would give the total number of Free Baptists in New Brunswick, in 1901, as 16,116, of whom eleven are recorded in the scnedules as Free Will Baptists.
In your letter to myself, as well as In your contribution to Dr. Saunder's History of Maritime Baptists, you have claimed that the total Free Baptists in New Brunswick, according to the recent census, shows a falling off in the number of about 10,300 and for the whole .Gnm-rion about 20,000 since 1891, and it is only reasonable that you should seek to ascertain the cause of this change. In your letter of June 5, 1902, you wrote :
' We are very anxious to discover the cause of the falling off which1 appears on the face of the returns, hut which we do not believe exists in fact. Kindly let me know if there is not some way of having the schedules which show the strange state of things which you mention pass under the eye of some one who knows the people as classified.'	.
I sympathized with you in your desire in this matter and although I could not under the regulations governing the census office allow the schedules to go into other hands, I took all reasonable means .to investigate the cause of the discrepancy in the number of your people for the two census years. But before proceeding to state the result, I think it is proper to mention a few facts which bear upon it.
1. An examination of the schedules showed that there were many kinds of Baptists in the maritime provinces and in the other provinces of Canada, and for publication purposes if was necessary to resort to grouping. Referring to the previous census reports since confederation we found that Baptists were classed under two general heads, namely, Baptists and Free Will Baptists. A few of the names of Baptist sects were unfamiliar to myself, as are indeed many of the 160 odd religious sects des-ribed in the schedules. For the bulletin on religions we followed the old headines, and I have to thank yourself for calling attention to the fact
that in the maritime provinces Free Baptist is the proper designation of the body formerly classed as Free Will. In Ontario, where I have always lived, persons of that belief have been known as Free Will Baptists, and I have known of them from my earliest years. Your letter, however, led me to make careful inquiry.
2.	I have found that in Nova Scotia the Free Will Baptists and the Free Christian Baptists agreed to unite into one body under the name of Free Baptists in 1867, and that in 1870 they were incorporated as one body under that name by an Act of the legislature.
3.	I found that the body known as Free Christian Baptists in New Brunswick was incorporated in 1854 under that name by the legislature of the province and that the name continued down to 1898, when by an amending Act it was changed to Free Baptists.
4.	I found that about the year 1874, under the leadership of Rev. G. W. Orser, a number of churches of Free Christian Baptists in New Brunswick separated from the parent body and assumed the name of Free Baptists, but commonly known as Orserites. This body applied for incorporation also in 1898 unaer the name of the Free Baptist denomination, and in their petition to the legislature they represented that they had existed separate and apart from the Free Christian Baptist General Conference for the previous twenty-three years as an organized body under the name of the Free Baptist denomination. But the legislature saw fit to deny them this title and incorporated them under the name of Primitive Baptists. In their treaties of faith published in 11S86, they are described as the Free Baptists of New Brunswick, Maine and Nova Scotia.
5.	I found also that another body had been formed out of the Free Christian Baptists under the name of Reformed Baptists, whose leading doctrine was belief in entire instantaneous sanctification, that they had been expelled from the Free Christian Baptist Conference of New Brunswick, and had ieen joined by a number of Free Baptists in Nova Scotia, and that in 1894 they secured incorporation from the parliament of Canada under the name of the Alliance of the Reform Baptist Church of Canada.
These facts must be familiar to you from your position as a leader in the body now known as the Free Baptists of New Brunswick, and no doubt it has often occurred to you as strange that in the successive censuses of Canada prior to 1891, the name Free Will Baptist was used to designate all Baptists of Armenian faith in the maritime provinces, although the large majority in the bodies there have for many years been known either as Free Baptists or Free Christian Baptists, but wh'at does not appear to have occurred to you is the probability that all these bodies were grouped together as Free Will Baptists including the two which had separated from your own conference, one by voluntary act and the other by expulsion. This probably did not occur to myself until recently, and then I proceeded to revise the census of Baptists in New Brunswick as taken in 1891. The work has been completed, and I will give you the results insofar as they concern your own body.
The schedules of the census of 1891 show for New Brunswick fifteen bodies of Baptists according to their descriptive names, and in the census volume they were grouped under the common heads of Baptists and Free Will Baptists, in our revised compilation we have separated these several bodies and the table which follows gives by census districts the number of Free Christian

Baptists and o! free Baptists. (The new name of the body given by the Act of 1898) with the otiect of showing exactly the relative strength of this body in the two census years.
Now, this is taken from the schedule of the two censuses of 1S91 and 1901, the exact statement of the people given to the enumerators of the church to whicli they lie-longed. In 1891 there were 10,072 who told the enumerators they belonged to the Free Christian Baptists in 1891, and in 10CL there were 16,105 who told the enumerators that they were Free Baptists. This shows therefore that in the particular branch about which Mr. McLeod is corresponding, there was an increase from 10,072 to 10,105, though by the grouping of other branches with the Free Christian Baptists of 1891, there appeared to he in that branch of Baptists, 24,000.
We have discovered .two errors in the tabulation of 1901 (as I have already stated), both due to the carelessness of a clerk in making up the . table from the compilation sheets. The first is in King's county, where 290 (Orserite) Baptists and one Old Baptist were added to Free Baptists instead of two Baptists. The second is in York county where 472 Free Christian Baptists were added to Calvinistic Baptists and grouped in the table with Baptists. These last are in the town of Marysville. Eleven persons were recorded in the schedule as Free Will Baptists and were added to Free Baptists in a. printed volume. But they are not included in the foregoing table.
In the census of 1891, the number of Free Will Baptists in the province as shown by the revised compilation of the schedules was 8,549, and all but eleven have disappeared by the showing of the recent census. We have, of course, no means of ascertaining what has become of them, but. the probability is that they have been merged with other Baptist bodies in the pio-vince. In the province of Ontario in 1891 there were 7,869 Free Will Baptists, and in the census of 1901. there were only thirty-nine.
I think Sir, it must be obvious from these statements that you have no just cause of complaint. You are certainly mistaken in assuming that the Free Baptist body of New Brunswick (formerly the Free Christian Baptist body) numbered 24.674 in 1891, and consequently you are mistaken in stating, as you have done in the letter to myself of May 3, 1902, and later in a chapter contributed to the Rev. Dr. Saunders History, that in our census they are made to lose about 10,000 in New Brunswick and in the Dominion at large about 20,000 in the ten years. The table I have given shows that in New Brunswick your body has made a gain of 5,433 instead of a large loss.
We had no other object than to give the numbers as they were collected by enumerators, and the instructions to enumerators for taking the religious census of the people were so clear and definite that I think it could not he misread or misunderstood.
Letters received from many enumerators state that great care was taken by them to record the religions of the people as they were given, and if mistakes have been made the strong probability is that the people themselves are to hlame. One fact deserving of special mention is that 1.338 persons counted in our volume as Free Baptists were recorded in the schedules as Free Christian Baptists, although the Act which

changed the name of that body was passed three years before the census was taken.
That is, I think, a complete explanation of the situation, and accounts fully for the apparent discrepancy which the Reverend Mr. McLeod complained of.

One of the results, evidently, of this trouble is that the theological knowledge of Mr. Blue seems to be considerably extended. He has evidently made some study of the Baptist denomination. I do not think that this statement at all answers the case that Mr. McLeod has made out. Take the parish of Kars, in the county of King's, X.B. In that parish there are no persons given as Free Baptists in the census, although there are two churches of that denomination in the parish. There are 100 communicants, and as the communicants are, as a rule, the heads of families, it would mean a population of at least 300 people professing that faith or belonging to that denomination. Yet, according to the census returns, there are no persons of that denomination in the parish. It seems that something should be done to remedy this defect. What right has the census commissioner to group these different denominations under one heading, no matter how small a denomination may be ? That denomination In the province of New Brunswick comprises some 20,000 souls, and I do not think it is so very insignificant that it does not deserve to be mentioned in the census returns. It seems to me that these people have not been treated with that justice which they should have received at the hands of the census commissioner. If he has made a mistake, and if his enumerators have not done their duty, it is his duty to remedy that mistake. It casts a certain amount of suspicion upon the genuineness of the whole census when we find such a glaring error as this cropping up, and it accentuates still more_ the errors that have been made in the taking of this census, for which we have paid over a million dollars, and the end is not yet.
They have not got through with the census yet.

No ; and if they undertake to correct the errors which have been made, it will take them until the time for a new census arrives before they get through with it. I think it is the duty of the hon. minister to go into this matter. Now that lie has returned from foreign parts and is once more with us, I think he should devote his great mind to the straightening out of this affair. Evidently the commissioner is not equal to the task, and I think the hon. minister should take a hand in it, and see that this province down by the sea gets justice.

There is no desire to obtain anything except the truth in regard to these census returns. When the instructions were sent out

the enumerators were asked to study them carefuly and to carry out their requirements. When the compilation was made in the bureau at Ottawa the information supplied was the information contained in the schedules. That information was acted upon, and the compilation was made strictly upon the information supplied by the enumerators. If, when an enumerator went to a person in New Brunswick and asked him the religious denomination to which he belonged and he refilled that he was a Baptist, he would be put down as a Baptist; if he replied that he was a Free Will Baptist, he would be put down as a Free Will Baptist, and if lie replied that he was a Free Baptist, he would be put down as a Free Baptist.

Does the hon. minister suppose that these people in the parish of Kars, who are very intelligent people, gave their religious denomination as Baptists, knowing that they belonged to the Free Baptist denomination ?

I can only suppose that the people gave the answer to the census enumerator which they considered to be correct, and if they gave themselves as Baptists, the enumerator would put them down as Baptists.

These people know the sharp distinction there is between the Free Baptist denomination and the Baptist denomination, and that the only thing they have in common, as I understand, denominationally, is the general belief that ail Christians have. So far as church government is concerned, and except so far as the ordinance of baptism by immersion is concerned, they are as distinct from the Baptists as the Methodists are from the Presbyterians, and that these people would give themselves as Baptists is an absurd contention. The difficulty arose out of the ignorance of the enumerators that were appointed. These people, of course, gave themselves as Free Baptists, but the enumerators did not think it made any difference, and they put them down as Baptists.

That is an explanation which, I confess, I never believed possible. I never believed that when one person said that he was a Free Baptist and another person said that he was a Baptist, the enumerator would ignorantly put down the person who said that he was a Free Baptist as a Baptist.
Is it not more reasonable to suppose that than that these people were so ignorant that they did not know the denomination to which they belonged 1
1 am just informed of what I did not know before, that, as a matter of fact, in the census return there is not one single Free Baptist put down in Kars.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) stated that.
Yes, that is what I have stated.
I cannot explain that, except upon the supposition that the people there who call themselves Free Baptists called themselves merely Baptists to the enumerator without putting in the adjective.
No ; the two denominations exist there, and those people who are Free Baptists would not call themselves Baptists.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) know that they are what are called Free Baptists now, because, as the lion. Minister of Agriculture pointed out, there were a number of divisions of the Baptist body and it occurred to me that perhaps one of these divisions did not amalgamate with the body now known as Free Baptists ? It does seem a most extraordinary thing that if there were two churches known to belong to the Free Baptist body, the enumerator failed to find a single Baptist in that district, That is beyond understanding. It occurs to me that perhaps these churches were attached to other bodies that did not amalgamate, but of course I do not know the facts.

I had the honour of a seat in the New Brunswick legislature at the time the Act was passed, and there was a Free Baptist body and this body that the minister has spoken of calling themselves Orserites, a sort of off shoot from the Free Christian Baptist body which was the old name. By the Act of the legislature in 1898 the name was changed to Free Baptist, and I think the Orserites went under the name of Christian Baptists. These two churches belonged to the Free Baptist body having one clergyman for the two churches, and he is a Clergyman of the Free Baptist denomination. The census of Kars was taken by a man named Jenkins and knowing Mr. Jenkins as well as I do, I am satisfied that he is the mail who made the blunder and put these people down as Baptists although they told him they belonged to the Free Baptist denomination. As I understand, Mr. Blue was written to especially nbout this case and he said he would call the attention of Mr. Jenkins to this, and that there was going to be a revision of the whole census relating to the religion of the people of New Brunswick. The Rev. Dr. McLeod wrote afterwards to this man Jenkins and Jenkins refused to make any change.

Mr. Jenkins was perfectly justified in that because under his oath of office he is forbidden to divulge any information lie got. I am informed that Mr. Blue received no letter from the Rev. Mr. McLeod in relation

to this particular parish of Kars, and that there is no letter in relation to this particular matter in the department at all. There have been references to it in a paper which is edited by Mr. McLeod, but neither Mr. McLeod, nor any one else drew Mr. Blue's attention to this particular case.

I will read from a letter
which I have received from Mr. McLeod.
In the parish of Kars, King's county, there are two Free Baptist congregations. The communicants in the churches number over one hundred, and the adherents number probably three hundred, or more.
The census fails to record a single one of them. Mr. Blue's attention was called to the matter some months ago. He professes to have made a revision of the whole census relating to the religions of the people in New Brunswick, but has made no change in the Kars enumeration.
Since Mr. Blue reported the result of his so-called revision, I have had correspondence with Mr. M. Jenkins, the Kars enumerator and he tells me he entered all Free Baptists as Baptists. I concluded, therefrom that Mr. Blue did net. as he pretends, ask Mr. Jenkins to revise his enumeration. Either Blue did not ask Jenkins to correct his returns, or Jenkins refused to do it.

Mr. McLeod possibly refers to what lias appeared in tlie * Religious Intelligencer,' but I can state positively that Mr. McLeod did not draw Mr. Blue's attention to the parish of Kars in a letter. He did draw Mr. Blue's attention to the general question of the Baptist denomination in New Brunswick, but be gave no details with regard to Kars. He made general statements the substance of which is in the letter which I read.
Have you published the revised statement ?

I will explain that Mr. Blue went to work to revise the compilation, and the revision that Mr. McLeod refers to in the letter was a revision of the compilation. Mr. Blue did not undertake to make inquiries from every enumerator in every instance. He did in several instances, and the replies were that the information contained in the schedules was exactly what the people gave them. It would be an entirely different thing to go to the people and take a new enumeration, and I confess that I am not prepared to say that ought to be done in any case. If the people did give information to the enumerators which they wished to change afterwards, or which other people wished to pursuade them to change, it is not the duty of the census bureau to get the whole work done over again by the enumerators. If the information given is not correctly set down by the enumerators then there would be a case for investigation. If the people called themselves Free Baptists, and were entered as Baptists

then the enumerators did not do their duty and the schedules being incorrect the compilation would also be Incorrect. What investigation we have made would go 'to show that the enumerators did actually put down what the people told them. Nothing has been brought to the attention of the department, beyond the general statement by Mr. McLeod, that indicated that the people had been misrepresented in the schedules.

The people do not see the schedules and consequently they could not tell that they were misrepresented. In the city of St. John the Free Baptist denomination has two large churches, and some of the members of that denomination occupy foremost positions. They are a very intelligent and cultured people-one of the judges of the Supreme Court belongs to that denomination, and they are not ashamed of belonging to the denomination and St. John being the centre of culture and of light and learning in our province, it is clear that they would tell the enumerators to what denomination they belonged. Nevertheless we find there are only 410 Free Baptists in St. John according to the census. Yet the actual population as taken by the clergymen amounts to 1,826, or about one twenty-fifth of the whole population of the city. So that there is clearly some error.

I am perfectly prepared to say, in consequence of what the hon. gentleman has said tonight about the parish of Kars, that I shall certainly see that a thorough investigation of the condition of affairs there is made, and shall try to get at the actual truth. If the enumerator has done as the hon. gentleman states, misrepresented the statements as given by the people themselves, he certainly has not fulfilled his duty as an enumerator, and has done a wrong to the people there. I shall try to find out the facts of the case.

As a matter of fact this letter states :
I have had correspondence with Mr. M. Jenkins. the Kars enumerator, and he tells me that he entered all Free Baptists as Baptists.
He does not claim that these people represented themselves as Baptists, but be says he entered all Free Baptists as Baptists, which was clearly a wrong, because it was his duty to enter these people as they called themselves. I have no doubt the enumerators in the city of St. John have done exactly the same thing.

I say I am perfectly prepared to make an investigation into any matter, which comes before the department, in the form in which the hon. gentleman brings it up, for the first time to-night. The statement made In

4S14
that letter that Mr. McLeod had drawn Mr. Blue's attention to this particular parish is not correct. I have looked over a file of the 1 Religious Intelligencer,' and the first reference I find in it to the parish of Kars is on May 13th. It was only yesterday that I first saw that. But the statement that Mr. McLeod had himself drawn the attention of Mr. Blue to that particular parish is not correct. There is nothing in the correspondence between Mr. McLeod and Mr. Blue with reference to the parish of Kars at all.
Perhaps you have not seen that part of the correspondence. Perhaps Mr. Blue has not called your attention to that.
I have seen the whole of the correspondence.

Mr. McLeod, in his letter to me, says :
The census fails to record a single one of them. Mr. Blue's attention was called to the matter some months ago.
I take that to mean the parish of Kars.
The context would seem to make it mean that.
But that does not accord with the facts.
What steps does the minister intend to take to remedy this ?

I shall have to look into the matter. I shall take that particular parish, find what the enumerator's statement is in regard to it, and examine him and see whether he put down the people under the name of the Christian denomination which they gave him. If. as that letter states he says, he entered them as Baptists when as a matter of fact they called themselves Free Baptists, he will show that he did not fulfil his duty as an enumerator.
Suppose you find that he did that, what will you do with him ?

I do not quite know what I will do with him. I shall have to look into the matter, and if I find that to be the case, have the census return corrected. Of course, the census volumes the past year have already been published.
Is the census complete now ?
That portion of it is completed, and is published. I may have to issue a supplementary report.
The same thing occurred in St. John.

I will do the same with reference to St. John,
and in any other case in which a definite statement is made in regard to the conduct of the enumerators. I am going to defend my officers, but if any accusation is made against them, I will investigate it, and if they are proved to have done wrong, they will have to suffer the consequences. I propose to have the census made as correct as I can.

Of course, it is important that we should have a correct census. If it was considered important to have a question asked as to the religious denomination of a person, it is important that the answer recorded should be the correct one. That is even more important than that the hon. minister should defend his officers.
Certainly. What I mean is that I do not want my officers to lie under an imputation, and for that reason alone I will make an investigation.

The hon. minister will see that somebody has blundered, and I would suggest that when he comes to make a thorough investigation into this matter, if his officer states that he has done right, and has actually put down in the schedules the religious denomination given by the people themselves, he should give the people who complain an opportunity of proving that officer is now making a wrong statement to the department. You must not take the statement of your officer, in whom you have explicit confidence-and rightly so until you find that he is wrong-you must not take his statement as being correct without giving the other party a chance to show that the officer is making a misstatement.
Of course, if my officer stands in the position of the accused party, I am not going to take his statement as conclusive.

I take a deep interest in this matter because, in the first place, in common with all the members, I desire that we should have an accurate census, and in the second place because I represent a greater number of Free Baptists than any other member from the maritime provinces.
Do they vote for you ?

They are a very intelligent body of men, and I think they vote right. They are the second largest religious body in my constituency, and I am glad to know that I have heard no complaint whatever from them about any difficulty in connection with the census. I did have a letter from one who said that there was some complaint in New Brunswick, and hoped that it would be made right. There is another reason -why I should feel much

interested in this matter. A portion of | this correspondence occurred while I was acting for the Minister of Agriculture during his absence, and I took occasion to look over it, and I certainly had the impression, not that Mr. Blue was curt towards the reverend gentleman, but that he endeavoured to meet his views and give him all the information possible. It is quite evident that in the census of 1891, a number of religious bodies were grouped together, thereby giving a larger number than should have been given under one head. Therefore I am afraid that a comparison with the census of 1891 does not help us. Our concern is not with the census of 1891, but with the census of 1901. The statement with regard to the parish of Kars is new to me, and if there are two churches of that body there and the census enumerator does not return a single member, I cannot conceive of any explanation of the matter. I quite agree that the minister should look into that and try to ascertain the cause of complaint. It would be very strange indeed if the enumerators scattered over New Brunswick should particularly err with regard to that body. The case of Kars needs investigati n and also St. John, but I think that the -hon. gentleman will find that the general reduction which caused the correspondence must be due to the fact that in 1891 there were grouped under that head a number of people who did not call themselves Free Baptists.

I do not think that this grouping business will account for the falling off, because the people who are called Free Christian Baptists in 1891 and are now Reformed Baptists, represent seventy-five or eighty per cent of the whole. I trust that the hon. minister will have this matter looked into and a correction made.

As regards those other bodies being inconsiderable, they were fully one-third of the whole number of 24,000 odd. A little over one-third were reported as Free Will Baptists in 1891. The Reformed Baptists and Alliance Baptists bodies were not included under the head of Free Will Baptists in 1901. In making this investigation, Mr. Blue took the evidence he had under his hand in the schedules of 1891 and 1901. When he investigated the schedules of 1891, he found 24.000 under the head of Free Will Baptists, and he found that the two denominations of Baptists, which were not included in that same heading of 1901, comprised just a little over one-third of the whole number. In the complaint made by Mr. McLeod to Mr. Blue, there is nothing to show that the enumerators had not correctly entered the people they enumerated. Mr. McLeod drew attention to the extraordinary apparent decrease of that particular branch of the Baptist denomination in ten years, but in the investigation which Mr. Blue carried on, that decrease was en-Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
| tirely accounted for and the Census Bureau did not deem it necessary to go further.
Does the census of 1901 show this Reformed Baptist body V
No, they put it under the head of Baptists and not Free Will Baptists. They are grouped with the other Baptist denominations and not with the Free Will Baptists.

I find that in the riding of East Simeoe there was in 1891 only one so-called commissioner, whose fees were about half the fees of the two commissioners in 1901, and in North Ontario we find also two commissioners in 1901 as against one in 1891. Can the hon. minister explain why there is this enormous difference in this one county of nearly 85,000, and will he assure the House that the census of 1901 will have information which will justify this increased expenditure ?

I think that my hon. friend was answered already on several occasions in connection with the census. I am satisfied that the mass of information we have received in tliis census is quite sufficient to justify the difference in the cost. I have explained the reasons and am afraid I cannot add very much to them now. The first reason applies to almost every county in the Dominion.
Can the hon. gentleman state any particularly valuable information in the census of 1901 which is not in the census of 1891V
I can give one instance on the spur of the moment. We have in the census of 1901 the value of all our agricultural products and that was not in the census of 1891.
What proportion of the increase would that account for ?

It is difficult to say what proportion:	The
number of questions was largely increased by that fact as well as by a large number of other facts. I have already explained to the House over and over again the much greater number of questions that we asked, and these are some of them. There are other things on which the number of questions was largely increased. That accounts for the large proportion of the increased

expense, for it took the enumerators more time, and caused them greater labour to get the answers to these questions, and they had to be paid on a larger scale. The other details I have given. While I am on my feet I would like to answer the question asked by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor). In 1891 there were 79,634 of all Baptists in the province of New Brunswick, and in 1901 there were 80,874, a trifling increase in the whole Baptist denomination in tiie province of New' Brunswick.
Were the enumerators paid by the day or by the questions they asked ?
Neither, but by a schedule of rates, which rates were increased because of the number of questions.
A schedule of what ?
A schedule of rates for the names they took, the houses, farms, factories, and so on.
If they were not paid by the questions they asked, how was it they got more ?
The schedule of rates was higher in consequence of the number of questions asked.

Exactly what I say- they were paid by the number of questions
they asked. Was there a rate for horse-hire or were the enumerators allowed to charge as they liked ?
There was a rate.
Was the same rate allowed in all the towns and villages ?
Yes, wherever the rate was allowed at all.
What are ive to understand hy that ? I asked the minister a plain question-was the same rate allowed in all the villages and towns ?
I cannot answer that question, because, as a general rule there was not a rate allowed in the towns or villages.

Here is an illustration of how the country is being fleeced by some of the enumerators. What check was there on unscrupulous men charging nearly as much for horse-hire as for their own wages 7 Take the village of Brighton. We have three enumerators there. One of them, whose wages amounted to $24.05, charged for horse-hire, 822.50.
Will the hon. gentleman give me the page from which he has quoted 7

The Auditor General's Report, page D-183. In the village of I
Brighton there are only about 1,300 people. Then we have the village of Campbellford, a much larger place, with a large enough population in fact, to be incorporated as a town, and you find that only one enumerator was allowed horse-hire, and that one was allowed $1.50. Go through the Auditor General's Report and you will find the same thing-you will find some charging as much for horse-liire as for taking .the census, while others are allowed nothing. Why should a man be allowed horse-hire for taking the census in a little village 7 I am satisfied that thousands of dollars have been spent in this way for the benefit of Grit heelers. I know' this man well.
Is he a good Grit 7

Yes, if there are any good Grits. I know a good many Reformers, and I respect them; but when you call a man a Grit, I do not think there are any good ones. They are good at fleecing the public, that is all they are good for. Mr. Smith, to whom this allowance was made, is a farmer in the township of Brighton, and he was appointed to take the census in the village of Brighton. Why 7 There are intelligent men in the village of Brighton who could have taken the census, but, instead, this man is taken out of the township to take the census of Brighton village, and I suppose he had to drive in and put up his horse in the stable and the people of Canada pay for it. We see the same kind of thing in many other cases, and this, to my mind, is the real reason why the expense of taking the census is so great.

I have not under my hand the account rereferred to by the hon. gentleman. Horse-liire vras allowed to enumerators who had to leave their homes in order to take the census. As a rule there was an enumerator for each polling subdivision, and the rule was to appoint a man for the polling subdivision in which he lived. The polling division in a village might extend into the country, or a part of the division be in the village and the enumerator live in the country. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) said that this enumerator lived out in the country.
Yes, and why did the hon. minister appoint a man who lived o*ut in the country to take the census in the village 7
I cannot say.

Then, what does the hon. minister suppose the inference will be 7 It looks very much as if this man were a Grit heeler. Among the people of Brighton are men quite competent to take the census, far more intelligent than this man who urns appointed, no doubt to reward him for

some of the dirty work he had done for the party.
That was not the purpose, certainly, whatever he may be. The rule laid down was-
Why did you not carry it out ? What is the good of a rule if you do not carry it out ?

My information is that it was carried out. The commissioners had to pass upon the accounts after they had been submitted with a declaration by the people who made them, and they had to be passed upon by the commissioners for the riding, who knew all the circumstances. When they were sent ill approved in this way they were gone over by the accountant of the department, before being paid. Then they were sent over by the Auditor General to be further scrutinized. And, so far aa I know, no fault has been found with these accounts.

Did they make sworn returns ?
The' MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE. They took an oath that all their returns would be in accordance with the facts. That general oath would cover their accounts.
That was their oath of office ?
Yes.
Did they submit their statements under oath ?

They made a declaration as to the truth of their accounts and that declaration is attached to the account. It was sent to the commissioner for the riding, who made a declaration and sent it to the accountant.

How does the hon. gentleman account for there being this high charge for horse-hire in the village of Brighton ? The other men living in the village, men that I know well, got only $7.50. How could there be any scrutiny of the accounts at all, or any rule, when we see that discrepancy in two villages in the one riding, and the little village of Hastings, with less than 1,000 inhabitants, where these gentlemen get horse-hire ? They did not get any more information in Campbellford than they did in Brighton, or any more in Brighton than they did in Campbellford. Yet we find that $22.50 is paid for horse-hire in Brighton and none at all in Campbellford.
In addition to their work as enumerators, they were allowed horse-hire when they went to receive their instructions from the commissioner of the county.
That is a uniform rate all through the census, $9.

They were allowed $3 a day and their travelling expenses, and if they travelled with a horse they were allowed $1.50 for the horse. They were also allowed travelling expenses in going to make their returns to the census commissioner.
The special allowance all through this volume is $9.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken, the uniform allowance is $3 a day, but sometimes they charged for three days where they were entitled to do so.
On both pages here I find it is $9 for expenses in East Northumberland and West Northumberland-it is uniform.
Why were they paid $9 in some places and $6 in others ?
In some cases they took three days to receive their instructions and in some cases two days.
In the county of Frontenac $0 is the uniform allowance paid, while in my county $9 was paid.
It is evident the enumerator took two days to get his instructions in Frontenac and three days in the hon. gentleman's county.

I see an item on page D-282, ' Investigating census of 1891, $1,480. D. F. Macpherson, Clinton, Ont., expenses of trip to Ottawa to receive instructions, and in riding obtaining information, including payment to persons consulted, $73.95 ; 57 days time at $5, $358.95.' I would like the minister to give us an explanation why a gentleman was invited down from Clinton, Ont., to Ottawa, and how it comes that he was allowed to pay people in his county for information they were asked to give him.

He was brought down to Ottawa to be given instructions as to what he should do, and for the purpose of going over the schedules that were in the department here, which would be a guide to him in his investigations.
What was the nature of these investigations ?
To see whether the census returns of 1891 included the names of people who were not in the country, but who were permanently away.
What was the object of that ?

Because statements were made very generally that the census of 1901 showed that the census of 1891 could not have been correct, therefore it was necessary to investigate the census of 1891 to see whether the error was made then or in 1901.
In how many counties did Mr. Macplierson make the investigation ?
I think in four or five ridings in Ontario. There was a report laid on the Table last session.

The hon. gentleman said that he proposed to revise the census of the religious denominations in some parishes of New Brunswick. I would like to know if he is going to apply that revision to the province of New Brunswick generally, or only to the parishes indicated to the hon. member for King's (Mr. Fowler). I may say that in the parish of Lincoln, where I reside, I believe that nearly 70 per cent of the population belong to the Free Baptist denomination. From the best authority I can get, they have not been classified as Free Baptists. As the hon. member for King's has stated, they are an important denomination, there being 20,000 of them in that province, and I think they should have some recognition in the census. I do not think there has been any wilful wrong done in the matter, but a mistake has evidently been committed. In the case of so important a denomination, the enumerators should have been instructed to classify them. From the information I can gather, the enumerators went through their districts and asked the religious denomination of the people, whether they were Free Baptists, or Close Communion Baptists, or any other kind of Baptists, but they did not classify them, and they put them all down as Baptists. I think the department, in view of the standing of that denomination, should have provided a distinct classification for them. The Finance Minister has stated that he also has a large portion of that denomination in his constituency.
We are both very fortunate.

I think I can vie with the minister in that distinction as a very large portion of my constituency belong to that denomination, and in the county of Sunbury a large portion of the people are Free Baptists. As I said before, in the parish of Lincoln, I venture to say 70 per cent of the people belong to the Free Baptist denomination. I will add that when the minister revises his list he had better include the county of Sunbury and Queen's, and indeed I would recommend him to extend his investigations over the whole province.

I am ready to investigate any place where a '
definite statement is made that there has been an inaccurate return.
I would draw the attention of the minister to the township of Ilaldimand, West Northumberland, containing twelve polling subdivisions.
What page ?

D-184. The polling subdivisions are very small. In the township of Haldimand it is not much larger than Seymour, and there are items here of $26.65 for services, and $44.50 for horse-hire. There was no supervision of these charges at all. They put in their bills and got their money. The polling subdivisions are no larger than they are in the township of Seymour. There are 12 in Haldimand and in Seymour there are 5 or 6. There are no such charges in Seymour as-there are in the township of Haldimand.

I was going to say that I do not quite agree with my hon. friend from Sunbury and Queen's (Mr. Wilmot) that this was not deliberate and wilful. It is my opinion that the error on the part of the enumerators was both deliberate and wilful and that they should be very severely reprimanded by the hon. minister. If there is any punishment or reprimand in the power of the hon. minister I think these enumerators should be punished. I understand that the hon. minister proposes to extend the examination to the whole province of New Brunswick. Rev. Dr. McLeod is the editor of the organ of that denomination in New Brunswick, and I would suggest that the hon. minister communicate with him and get a statement from him as to the portion of the province which he thinks has not been properly enumerated, as regards the denomination which he represents and that he should extend his investigation into every portion of the province.
I would like to hear from the hon. minister if he has found that item ?
Yes, I see it here.
How does he account for that ? Did the horse get more information than the enumerator ?
I can only account for it by the fact that the enumerator must have gone over a very sparsely settled part of the country. I do not know the country as I never was there.
I do.

Then the hon. gentleman can account for it better than I can.
Mi-. COCHRANE. No, I cannot account for it except upon lines upon which I accounted for this other. The township Is

4S24
thickly populated. Tliis house did not travel any farther than any other horse in the township. The polling subdivisions are as equal in regard to size as they can be made by the municipal council. If the expense is to be judged by the information, and this is the reason the census costs nearly double the census of 1891, then, the only explanation is that the horse got more information than the enumerator did.
I would draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that the township has SI ,000 acres of land and that it only has a population of 3,900.
That is a mistake.
That is the result of the census.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think it goes to prove that the census returns are not correct. I drew the hon. minister's attention to the fact last session that in the town of Gan-anoque where we had the town assessor doing his work at the same time as the enumerators were taking the census, the assessor made the population 178 larger than the enumerators did and every person knows that the town assessor does not take the total of the residents.
In tlie town of Gananoque in 1001 the assessors made the population what ?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: 178. The hon. minister will find by reference to 'Hansard' of last session that I read certified statements from the town clerk that the assessment roll showed 178 more population than the enumerators' returns showed, and the count was taken practically on the same day. What I rose particularly for was to draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that I think he should take a new census not only for New Brunswick but for the whole Dominion, because, comparing the returns of the Free Baptists and the different branches of the Baptist denomination in New Brunswick for 1891 and for 1901, lie shows a very slight increase in the membership of that important church in the province of New Brunswick. The church must in the last ten years have made progress and it must have added some thousands of adherents. These additions are not in the census. This proves conclusively to my mind' that the census in New Brunswick is not correct in regard to these religious denominations and in regard to the total population. It is patent to any person, and and I think the hon. Minister of Finance, himself, will surely admit, that the Baptists have made some progress within the last ten years. Surely the church is not labouring there without making some progress. Ask the Rev. Dr. McLeod what increase has been made in the last ten years and he will make a showing very different from the in-

crease that the census shows. I am satisfied that the Baptist church in Canada has been making progress within the last ten years and that it has been gaining new adherents. I asked the hon. minister what was the total number of adherents of that church in 1S91 and in 1901 and lie gave a very few hundred of an increase. I cannot believe that the Baptist church or any other church professing to be a religious denomination in this country has not made progress greater than that shown from the census, because, otherwise, it would shut up shop and go out of business.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not intend to misquote me but the impression which he would leave would be an unfair one. The statement I read a few minutes ago showed that the Baptists in New Brunswick had increased by 1,000. The whole increase of population in the province is only 9,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Which proves that the census returns are not correct.
No, no.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am satisfied that the Baptists have increased more than that.
I find that this charge for instruction is not general. In King's County, New Brunswick nothing was charged at all for Instruction.
I notice that in King's, New Brunswick, there are no special allowance charges. There are no charges for horse-hire.
Very small charges.
I do not know why it was that there was no such charge sent in. We did not invite charges when they were not sent in.
How is it that the commissioner received $100 while in other counties, Kent for instance, the commissioners received $150.
Where there was one commissioner he was paid $100 and where there were two they were paid $75 each.
In Northumberland you paid $112 to each. What was the rate of pay in 1891 as compared with that in 1901 ?

In 1891; 3 cts. per name, 3 cts. per death, 15 cts. a farm, and 20 cts. a factory. In 1901; 5 cts. a name, 5 cts. a death, 25 cts. a farm, and 30 cts. a factory. No allowance for receiving instructions in 1891 and no liorse-hire.
Why were these additional allowances made.
The country was so prosperous and the rate of wages and the cost of living so much higher, that we could not get the work done without making this allowance.
In our county they were tumbling over each other to get the job.
Did the minister find any difficulty in getting people to act ?
Quite a little in places.
Name the places.
There were a number of people who refused.

It was not in the county of King's, New Brunswick, because they
were quarrelling for months before hand about it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Liberal committee had to ballot for them.

In East Simcoe there was an open fight as to who should be the commissioner, and the result was that two of them were tumbled into the job in order to bring about peace at an additional expense to the country. Why was Mr. Storey one of the commissioners, allowed a lump sum of $25 for expenses. If this money is given for sweet charity sake the people ought to know it.
Mr. Storey's account shows that he was allowed $75 as a commissioner and $25 for postage and the rent of a hall for instructions to the enumerators.
What was the rent of the hall.
The postage and hall rent are included together at $25.
Does the minister know what the rent of the hall was.
No.

I am glad the hon. minister told me that. If that is a sample of the way in which the country has been swindled out of its money the people should know it. This man is a practising lawyer and a police magistrate in the town, and so far as his hiring any hall goes it is absurd. It is a good deal on a par with a certain gentleman who, when they were taking the returns for the plebiscite-that old friend of the Minister of Agriculture-attempted to work in a grant of $25 for the rent of his office. I am glad to learn this from the minister and thank him for the information, because the people there will know they have been swindled out of their money.
Will the minister allow me to see that account for $25 for the rent of a hall for this commissioner.
Yes.
In North Ontario a gentleman named Duncan Graham, commissioner, got an allowance of $100 and $206.95 for revising the returns, and I understand that he can neither read nor write.
I should hardly think that is true.
He had a grit heeler as assistant commissioner, a gentleman that was concerned with ballot boxes in North Ontario on one occasion, a friend of the Postmaster General; a grit lawyer.
I do not know that gentleman.
He is a Grit lawyer of the name of Roach.
The commissioners are entitled to one cent for every name returned to them by the enumerators, and I find on looking up the matter that $206 is the payment for the names for that county.

That be-iug the case, I desire to draw the minister's attention to the Greys. For revising the returns of North Grey, the commissioner, R. B. Miller, received $188. The population of North Grey is 27,000 or more. The com-missoner of East Grey, Mr. Carruthers, received $253, and the population of that riding is 2,000 less than the population of North Grey. If they each received one cent per head, how do you account for that difference ? The cost of taking the census of East Grey was $3,592, while the cost of taking the census of North Grey, which has 2,000 more population, was only $3,000.

According to the population of East Grey the payment to the commissioner is correct, at one cent a name. The reason the commissioner of North Grey did not receive so much in proportion to the population of the riding is this : While each commissioner was entitled to receive one cent a name, no commissioner was allowed to receive more than $4 a day for every day of service. The commissioner of North Grey had forty-seven days of service, which at $4 a day made up the sum he actually received.

There is another matter on which I would like an explanation. J. Frost, of the town of Owen Sound, is down for $12 for horse-hire. I would like to know why he required horse-hire in taking the census of Owen Sound ?

I cannot say what that particular charge was for; but in some instances enumerators

in a town have been obliged for certain reasons to go out of town, and for that purpose have hired a horse. I remember one instance in which an enumerator in a town found that two or three people whom he had to enumerate were in the country, though properly residents of the town, and he had to drive out of town two or three miles to obtain the information which he was required to get. In such a case he would be justified in charging for horse-hire, and the case the hon. gentleman refers to may have been something like this.
This paper is an old-looking document. This man made out a bill for $100, and by somebody the $100 was changed to $75.
Because when there were two commissioners they could each receive only $75.

And then, it being found that he was going to be short, some person wrote in : ' Postage and hall rent, $25.' That is not in his handwriting, but was written in by -somebody else. He had to be placated, and somebody in the department here hit on this happy idea. Who does this grafting here ?
It does not appear to be in the same handwriting.
I should like to see that correspondence.
Will the minister explain what is the meaning of an assistant commissioner 7
In certain large areas the commissioners were given assistants, and it practically amounted to having another commissioner.
Were there many of these gentlemen having money thrust on them as this gentleman seems to have had 7
On the contrary, there was a very careful scrutiny of the accounts.

Does the hon. minister consider this a case of close scrutiny ? The commissioner sends in a bill for $100. It is impossible to allow him $100, so somebody in the department runs his pen through the $100 and makes it $75, and then adds $25 for lease of hall and postage. The other commissioner, Tudhope, was paid $125.
The hon. minister said that each could only get $75, but here is one getting $75 and the other $125.
I shall have to investigate that.

I would call attention to another difficulty in that famous riding of North Ontario. Mr. Duncan Graham was Hon. Mr. FISHER.
allowed $100 and a Mr. Roche $203 for fifty-eight days as assistant commissioner. Each of these got over $100.
North Ontario had only one commissioner.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Probably Graham could neither read nor write and required an assistant.
I do not know him, but I do not believe that he can neither read nor write. Mr. Roche was paid $203 for fifty-eight days' work.
Will the hon. minister let us have the Bill of Mr. Roche ?
I will look up the account and furnish it.
Are we to understand that $75 was the outside limit which any one of these commissioners was to get 7

There was a regular allowance of $75 where there were two commissioners, to each one for expenses. In addition each got one cent per name for all the names returned in the riding, but could not get more than $4 for

a day's work.
Did the hon. gentleman instruct Mr. Blue that no commissioner was to get more than $75 ?
That is the allowance for expenses, and in addition he got one cent per name but could not get more than $4 per day.
Why then did the department pay more 7
I do not know that it did except in the case of one commissioner, and he got $10).
In Northumberland county, N.B., two commissioners got $112 each. See page D-134 of the Auditor General's Report.
I am informed that there were one or two counties which were difficult and large, in which the allowance was increased. In Northumberland it was made $225 for the two commissioners instead of $150.	.
Northumberland is not the largest county in New Brunswick, Westmoreland has one-third more population than Northumberland.
Has it as large an area 7
Quite as large. A large portion of the county of Northumberland is forest.

I am informed that the county of Northumberland has an area of over 3,000,000 acres, and Westmoreland has about 1,000,000, so

that Northumberland is three times as large.

Will the hon. minister say whether his enumerators went through the forests of Northumberland ? Seventy-five per cent of Northumberland is forest, whereas Westmoreland is almost entirely settlement. The population of Northumberland is 30,000 and that of Westmoreland 45,000.
The hon. gentleman may be perfectly correct, but in a settlement where there is so much forest, the enumerators would have more difficulty in going through the forests.
But there is no population there.
There must be some population in every parish, and there are twelve different parishes.

There must be a population in every parish or it would not be a parish. A parish is a municipality. There is a vast forest, of course, which extends over the whole western portion of the county. The different parishes of the eastern part run into the west.
There is some settlement in the west ?
None at all. The enumerators would not go to the lumber camps.
Yes, if the lumber camps were in existence when the census was taken in April.
No, they would not be in the lumber camps then.
I did not know as to that, but if there were people in the camps, the enumerators would go there.

As a matter of fact where there are two or three commissioners, it is a mere matter of party exigencies. Is there not a uniform allowance in Ontario and Quebec of $100 for the commissioner for one cent per name for the commissioner ?
Where there was one. But where there is two, it was $75 and one cent a name.
Will the hon. minister say that two commissioners were appointed only where there were large areas to be gone over ?

There were various reasons-sometimes large areas, sometimes difficulty of access from one part of the riding to another, sometimes two nationalities in one constituency calling for the appointment of one commissioner for each nationality.

And sometimes none of these existed. Take, for instance, the. county of Elgin. There are uo mixed nationalities, no difficulty of areas, and it is ail old county and a small county, yet there were two commissioners.
I suppose one for East and one for West Elgin.
No, for West Elgin. The hon. gentleman has no escape of that kind. Then, what about the county of Wellington, what about the county of Wentworth ?
In the case of West Elgin part of the riding is in the county of Elgin and part of it is in the county of Kent, and a commissioner was appointed for each of these.

The hon. minister surely is beside himself. Does he not know that no notice was taken of municipal counties ? Does not he know that the census was taken by. electoral districts ? Surely his commissioner did not make the suggestion he has just communicated to us.
The reason is correct. In some cases where the electoral division was made up of two or three counties, two commissioners were appointed.
Then, take the county of Botliwell, which is made up of part of the county of Kent and part of the county of Lambton. Yet there was only one commissioner.	_
There might have been two.

North Victoria is made up of parts of three counties, yet the hon. minister appointed only one commissioner. He left out two heelers there. The hon. minister stated to the hon. member for King's, New Brunswick (Mr. Fowler) that he took the census for the lumber camps.
Yes.
So, these people will be counted twice.
No.
If, at a given house the enumerator were told that the husband and sons were working at a lumber camp, they would be enumerated there, and again in the lumber camp ?
No.	[DOT]
Then, why go to the lumber camp ?

If they were enumerated at the lumber

camp, the schedule of the lumber camp would be watched and, if the entries were duplicated they would be struck out in one.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I think the hour has arrived when we should rise.
I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) but some hon. gentlemen wish to get information, and I would ask them now to state what they want so that I may try to get it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)

speechtext:
And will the hon. minister please bring the account with respect to West Middlesex.
Progress reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: What will be the business for to-morrow ?

We shall probably take up several minor bills standing in the name of the Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick). At an early stage of the sitting there will be a motion for Supply to enable the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) to move his amendment.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 1.10 a.m. Wednesday.
Wednesday, June 17, 1903.
